children: Twenty-five years ago, Thomas B. Michaud arrived at KBW's offices in the World Trade Center later than usual. Today, now the investment bank's CEO, Michaud still draws on lessons from those early days.
By Thomas B. Michaud

On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, I missed my regular train and ended up in lower Manhattan later than usual. I had taken clients to a Michael Jackson concert the night before, and my four-year-old son surprised me in the shower the next morning. That delayed my daily commute to the World Trade Center, where I typically ran the morning call at the investment bank Keefe, Bruyette & Woods.
It was a clear day, I remember, with a crisp blue sky that offered no hint of the darkness to come.

Later that morning, KBW would lose 67 colleagues, including our co-CEO and five of our nine board members, who were working in our headquarters on the 88th and 89th floors of the South Tower. All of our records, technology, and infrastructure were destroyed in the terrorist attacks.

Twenty-five years later, people still ask me how the firm survived. The answer is simple. We relied on our values and on one another. Every day, we pushed the rock up the hill a little further. And we drew strength from something that had been built long before we ever needed it: a reservoir of goodwill.

In the days following the attacks, our phones began to ring. Clients called. Friends called. Competitors called. People offered office space, equipment, business opportunities, advice, introductions, and encouragement. They asked a simple question: What do you need?
Nobody asked what they would receive in return; people simply stepped up to help.
Looking back, that response is owed to KBW leadership's decadeslong commitment to building strong relationships.

Every organization accumulates different forms of capital. There is financial capital, intellectual capital, technological capital. But there is also human capital. Every interaction with a client, colleague, business partner, or community member either adds to or subtracts from a reservoir of goodwill. Organizations hope they never need to draw upon that reservoir. But when adversity arrives, they quickly discover whether or not it is full. Thankfully, ours was.

Our competitors became partners, clients became advocates, and colleagues became family. We witnessed an industry and a city come together around a shared belief that helping others was simply the right thing to do.

That spirit helped KBW rebuild. We quickly found new office space in Midtown Manhattan and began working there a few months later. Lower Manhattan rebuilt slowly, but now nearly as many people work there as did before the attacks. A new World Trade Center stands proudly on Fulton Street, 400 feet taller than the Twin Towers.
Much has changed in my life, too. I stepped up the leadership ladder and am now CEO of the firm. But I still draw on lessons from those early days:

Trust and relationships must be built before they are needed. The foundation of trust and relationships-credibility-must be established through thousands of small decisions, ethical choices, and commitments honored when no one is watching.

Resilience begins with determination but is sustained by relationships. The goodwill we create, the trust we earn, and the people we support matter way before a crisis and long after it has passed. In the end, organizations are measured not only by what they achieve but also by how they respond when adversity arrives. Strong cultures aren't created but revealed during crises.

One thing I have said often over the years is that I never want 9/11 to become just a few paragraphs in a history book. We must remember what happened that morning, but we should also remember what happened afterward. Because in the wake of one of the darkest days our country has experienced, we witnessed some of the very best humanity has to offer.
